name: Ruber
lede: Ruber is simply the Latin word for red, a solid basic color term in a language that struggled to name blue and yellow, and the root of the name Rubicon.

sections.title: Latin red
sections.body:
Pastoureau stresses that Latin red has a solid basic term, *ruber*, with a frequently used doublet *rubeus* that adds no particular nuance, and a rich supply of other red words [1][2]. Blue and yellow, by contrast, have no such basic term and are named through shifting vocabulary [1][3]. Black is split in two, matte *ater* and glossy *niger* [4].

Pastoureau also notes that the Romans treated *ruber* and *coloratus*, the word for colored, as synonyms, a sign of how central red dyeing was in the ancient world [5]. St Clair repeats that point [6]. Pastoureau ties this to the fact that for many millennia cloth was dyed mainly in red. It is a statement about vocabulary, not about any one dye.

sections.title: Red, strength and the Rubicon
sections.body: Pastoureau observes that Roman writers linked *ruber* to *robur*, the word for the oak and for strength, and saw red as the color of vigor, victory and power [2]. He also reads the name of the Rubicon, which Caesar crossed in 49 BCE, as formed from *ruber*, the river's waters being reddish because of the soil [2]. He gives it as the likely source of the name, not as a documented fact.

sections.title: Ruber in other places
sections.body: When medieval translators met Hebrew words meaning shining, Pastoureau says the Latin Bible sometimes gave *candidus* or *ruber*, a sign that the Latin translators added color words the Hebrew did not have [5]. Pastoureau dates the move from "color + adjective" phrases such as *color ruber* to plain color nouns to the 12th century, as vernacular languages took over [7]. Linnaeus kept *ruber* among his plant colors, and the scarlet ibis carries the Latin name *Eudocimus ruber* [8]. For the English colors descended from it see [[red]], [[scarlet]] and [[crimson]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The modern swatch #CE4676 is a pinkish red; it does not stand for Roman red, which the books never pin to one shade [1]. It matches a single painting in our archive of 23,781, a 1924 still life by Patrick Henry Bruce, covering about 12 percent of it, as photographed [9].
